source.module_title: Adam Clarke's Commentary and critical notes on the Bible

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen30455" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30456" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30457" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30457" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30456" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30458" type="x-p"/> The leading men, discrediting Jeremiah's prophecy, carry the people into Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.1-Jer.43.7">Jer 43:1-7</reference>. Jeremiah, by a type, foretells the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.8-Jer.43.13">Jer 43:8-13</reference>. This mode of conveying instruction by actions was very expressive, and frequently practiced by the prophets. The image of Nebuchadnezzar arraying himself with Egypt, as a shepherd puts on his garment, is very noble. Egypt at this time contended with Babylon for the empire of the east; yet this mighty kingdom, when God appoints the revolution, shifts its owner with as much ease as a shepherd removes his tent or garment, which the new proprietor has only to spread over him. See <reference osisRef="Jer.43.12">Jer 43:12</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30460" type="x-p"/> Men, and women, and children, and the king's daughters - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jer.41.10">Jer 41:10</reference> (note). It is truly surprising that the Chaldeans should have left behind any of the royal family of Judah! But, <div eID="gen30460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30461" type="x-p"/> 1. Perhaps they knew not there were any. <div eID="gen30461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30462" type="x-p"/> 2. If they did know, they might think, being children of concubines, they could not inherit. Or, <div eID="gen30462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30463" type="x-p"/> 3. That being females, they were not eligible. And they had taken care to seize all Zedekiah's sons, and slay them before his eyes.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30464" type="x-p"/> Came they even to Tahpanhes - This city was called Daphne by the Greeks, and was situated at the extremity of Lower Egypt, near to Heliopolis. It was called Daphne Pelusiaca. They halted at this place, most probably for the purpose of obtaining the king's permission to penetrate farther into Egypt. It was at this place that, according to St. Jerome, tradition says the faithful Jeremiah was stoned to death by these rebellious wretches; for whose welfare he had watched, prayed, gone through many indignities, and suffered every kind of hardship. And now he sealed the truth of his Divine mission with his blood.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30465" type="x-p"/> Take great stones - This discourse seems to have been delivered about a year after the destruction of Jerusalem. They pretended that they dared not stay in Judea for fear of the Chaldeans. The prophet here assures them that Nebuchadnezzar shall come to Egypt, extend his conquests in that kingdom, and place his tent over the very place where these stones were laid up, and destroy them. How these prophecies were fulfilled, see at the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.44.30">Jer 44:30</reference> (note).

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen30470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30471" type="x-p"/> He shall break also the images of Beth-shemesh - בית שמש beith shemesh is, literally, the house or temple of the sun; which was worshipped here, and whose images are said to have been of solid gold. These Nebuchadnezzar was to break and carry away; and the houses of the gods - all the temples of Egypt, he was to burn with fire. Beth-shemesh is the same as Heliopolis.  <chapter eID="Jer.43"/> <div eID="gen30471" type="x-p"/>
